description: The GOES-16 Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) L2 Cloud and Moisture Imagery provides 16 spectral bands with high temporal resolution over the American continent. The significance of the GOES-16 satellite for Brazil and South America lies in its location at longitude -75°, allowing it to offer comprehensive coverage of the continent and the oceanic regions of the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. The ABI captures 2 visible, 4 near-infrared, and 10 infrared channels at resolutions ranging from 500m to 2km. This collection encompasses images acquired by the GOES-16 satellite (GOES-East) in full-disk mode, depicting nearly full coverage of the Western Hemisphere in a circular image. Important: note that other modes, such as CONUS and MESOSCALE, are not included in this collection. Cloud and Moisture Imagery product (CMIP) files are generated for each of the 16 ABI reflective and emissive bands. The collection captures CMIP product files into individual STAC Items for each observation from the GOES-16 satellite. It includes the original and full-resolution CMIP NetCDF files generated by INPE's GOES-R receiving station. There is also a version for band 02, which originally has a resolution of 500m, degraded to 1km. For more information, refer to the [Beginner’s Guide to GOES-R Series Data](https://www.goesr.gov/downloads/resources/documents/Beginners_Guide_to_GOES-R_Series_Data.pdf), [GOES-R Series Product Definition and Users Guide: Volume 5 (Level 2A+ Products)](https://www.goes-r.gov/products/docs/PUG-L2+-vol5.pdf), [ABI Bands Quick Information Guides](https://www.goes-r.gov/mission/ABI-bands-quick-info.html) and the [GOES-R ABI Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document](https://www.star.nesdis.noaa.gov/goesr/documents/ATBDs/Enterprise/ATBD_Enterprise_Cloud_and_Moisture_Imagery_Product_v4_2021-01-13.pdf).
title: GOES-16 Cloud & Moisture Imagery

The entire earth is covered by 341 orbits during a 24-day cycle. The LISS-3 sensor covers a 140-km orbital swath at a spatial resolution of 24 meters with a 24-day repeat cycle. Level 2 products have radiometric correction and geometric correction using satellite ephemeris and attitude data (system correction).

description: GOES-13 is a satellite of the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) series operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Launched on May 24, 2006, it is designed to monitor weather conditions in North America, South America, and the Atlantic Ocean region. It operates in a geostationary orbit, meaning it remains fixed relative to Earth, continuously monitoring a specific region of the planet. In 2017, it was replaced by GOES-16 (GOES-East) as the primary operational weather satellite for the United States. Since then, it has been placed in a backup position. GOES-13/Imager instrument captures 1 visible and 4 infrared channels at resolutions of 1km (VIS) and 4km (IR). The collection captures product files into individual STAC Items for each observation from the GOES-13 satellite. It contains binary files in a grid format for each of the 5 spectral bands. The files are encoded using int16 and represent a matrix of values (reflectance for VIS and brightness temperature for IR) with 1714 lines and 1870 columns. Note: The values must be read as a one-dimensional array and then converted in memory to a two-dimensional m x n matrix. These versions are generated by INPE using the process of mapping data from the original geostationary projection to a uniform space-time geographic grid (EPSG:4326) with 0.04 degrees spatial resolution. The geographical area used in the remapping process was chosen because it covers and highlights Brazil, South and Central America. The image reprojection operation is performed using the gdalwarp utility (https://gdal.org/programs/gdalwarp.html) with the nearest neighbor resampling strategy defined.
title: GOES-13/Imager - Level-3 - VIS/IR Imagery (Binary)

description: The biogeochemical products (Chlorophyll-a, Suspended Particulate Matter, Particulate Organic Carbon, absorption by Colored Dissolved Organic Matter, and Dissolved Organic Carbon) are derived from remote sensing reflectance (Rrs, measured in sr⁻¹) retrieved from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) onboard NASA's Aqua satellite (MODIS-Aqua) and atmospherically corrected using the Ocean Color - Simultaneous Marine and Aerosol Retrieval Tool (OC-SMART) (Fan et al., 2021). These products are generated from daily Rrs observations with a nominal spatial resolution of 1 km at nadir. For each day, multiple MODIS-Aqua swath tiles covering the study area are processed individually to produce the corresponding Rrs. The resulting Rrs tiles are then merged into a single seamless daily mosaic using the SNAP Mosaicking Tool, producing a daily Rrs composite that combines all available observations for that day. The daily Rrs composites are subsequently used as input for the retrieval of the following biogeochemical products: • Chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL, mg·m⁻³): estimated using the Combination Of Neural Network models in Estimating Chlorophyll-a over Turbid and Clear Waters (CONNECT) algorithm (Tran et al., 2025). • Suspended Particulate Matter concentration (SPM, g·m⁻³): estimated using a blend of two SPM algorithms (Salah Salah et al., 2025). • Particulate Organic Carbon (POC, mg·m⁻³): estimated by combining the algorithms proposed by Loisel et al. (2002, 2018), Tran et al. (2016), and Le et al. (2016). • Absorption by Colored Dissolved Organic Matter (aCDOM, m⁻¹): estimated from the remote sensing reflectance band centered at 443 nm using the algorithm developed by Bonelli et al. (2021). • Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC, µmol·L⁻¹): estimated using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) machine-learning approach (Bonelli et al., 2022). The monthly biogeochemical products are subsequently generated by calculating the geometric mean of the corresponding daily biogeochemical products on a pixel-by-pixel basis over each calendar month, producing monthly composites for each biogeochemical variable.
title: MODIS-Aqua monthly biogeochemical products

description: Downward shortwave radiation flux (DSWRF) at the surface represents the solar energy incident on the Earth's surface. Various terms for this variable are found in the literature, including global solar radiation descending to the surface, where the term 'global' refers to total solar radiation, including direct radiation (arriving in line of sight from the solar disk) and diffuse radiation (solar radiation scattered by gases, clouds, and aerosols). Another term associated with its physical unit (W/m²) is global solar irradiance. The data are generated from instantaneous outputs inferred by GL1.2 model and visible channel images from GOES satellites (GOES-10, GOES-12, GOES-13, GOES-16, GOES-19). For each day, the instantaneous images are integrated using the trapezoidal rule, and the final value is divided by 24 hours to represent the daily mean irradiance (W/m²). Each daily data file is an image covering South America and the surrounding oceans. Each pixel in the image indicates the daily mean solar radiation. References: [G-STAR/INPE - Grupo de Radiação Solar, Terrestre e Atmosférica](https://satelite.cptec.inpe.br/gstar/GSTAR_principal.html); [GL1.2 Model](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2003JD003531).

description: South American Mapping of Temperature (SAMeT) is a newly developed product and operationally available for South America through the National Institute for Space Research (CPTEC / INPE) Weather Forecast and Climate Studies website. This product combines the observed data with the ERA5 reanalysis, making a correction of the temperature field using an estimated lapse rate. The Lapse Rate was estimated for four regions located over South America, and for the four seasons of the year. The estimated values for the Lapse Rate were, in all situations, lower than the standard Lapse Rate (-6.5 °C·km-¹). The combination of reanalysis and observations, together with the correction of the Lapse Rate produced more accurate temperature fields than those provided by ERA5, especially in regions with more accentuated topography.

description: The MODIS-Aqua Monthly Remote Sensing Reflectance (Rrs, unit sr-1) provides 8 spectral bands temporal resolution of one month and spatial resolution of 1 km over the Brazil oceanic waters and open ocean South Atlantic waters. This collection captures 7 visible, and 1 infrared channels using Level-1A images acquired from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) instrument onboard the NASA's Aqua satellite. The Level-1A data were processed into Level-1B and GEO using the Data Processing Tools (modis_L1B) from SeaWiFS Data Analysis System (SeaDAS) software. The Level-1B and GEO data were applied in the atmospheric correction OC-SMART (Fan et al., 2021) by the National Institute for Space Research (INPE, Brazil) and the Laboratoire d'Océanologie et de Géosciences (LOG, France) generating the Level-2 data. The Level-2 data has been mosaicked to generate daily maps capturing the complete Brazilian ocean waters. The daily mosaic data were reprojected to geographical (lat/lon) coordinates using as reference the European Space Agency (ESA) Ocean Colour - Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI) into Level-3 grid. Both, the mosaic and the reprojection were done using the Sentinel Application Platform (SNAP) on its version 10. Finally, the daily reprojected data were temporal merged to create the monthly Rrs products using the geometric mean.

description: The biogeochemical products (Chlorophyll-a, Suspended Particulate Matter, Particulate Organic Carbon, absorption by Colored Dissolved Organic Matter, and Dissolved Organic Carbon) are derived from remote sensing reflectance (Rrs, measured in sr⁻¹) retrieved from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) onboard NASA's Aqua satellite (MODIS-Aqua) and atmospherically corrected using the Ocean Color - Simultaneous Marine and Aerosol Retrieval Tool (OC-SMART) (Fan et al., 2021). These products are generated from daily Rrs observations with a nominal spatial resolution of 1 km at nadir. For each day, multiple MODIS-Aqua swath tiles covering the study area are processed individually to produce the corresponding Rrs. The resulting Rrs tiles are then merged into a single seamless daily mosaic using the SNAP Mosaicking Tool, producing a daily Rrs composite that combines all available observations for that day. The daily Rrs composites are subsequently used as input for the retrieval of the following biogeochemical products: • Chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL, mg·m⁻³): estimated using the Combination Of Neural Network models in Estimating Chlorophyll-a over Turbid and Clear Waters (CONNECT) algorithm (Tran et al., 2025). • Suspended Particulate Matter concentration (SPM, g·m⁻³): estimated using a blend of two SPM algorithms (Salah Salah et al., 2025). • Particulate Organic Carbon (POC, mg·m⁻³): estimated by combining the algorithms proposed by Loisel et al. (2002, 2018), Tran et al. (2016), and Le et al. (2016). • Absorption by Colored Dissolved Organic Matter (aCDOM, m⁻¹): estimated from the remote sensing reflectance band centered at 443 nm using the algorithm developed by Bonelli et al. (2021). • Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC, µmol·L⁻¹): estimated using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) machine-learning approach (Bonelli et al., 2022).
title: MODIS-Aqua daily biogeochemical products

description: The MODIS-Aqua Daily Remote Sensing Reflectance (Rrs, unit sr-1) provides 8 spectral bands, temporal resolution of one month, and spatial resolution of 1 km over the Brazilian oceanic waters and the open ocean South Atlantic waters. This collection captures 7 visible and 1 infrared channels using Level-1A images acquired from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) instrument onboard NASA's Aqua satellite. The Level-1A data were processed into Level-1B and GEO using the Data Processing Tools (modis_L1B) from SeaWiFS Data Analysis System (SeaDAS) software. The Level-1B and GEO data were applied in the atmospheric correction OC-SMART (Fan et al., 2021) by the National Institute for Space Research (INPE, Brazil) and the Laboratoire d'Océanologie et de Géosciences (LOG, France), generating the Level-2 data. The Level-2 data has been mosaicked to generate daily maps capturing the complete Brazilian ocean waters. The daily mosaic data were reprojected to geographical (lat/lon) coordinates using the European Space Agency (ESA) Ocean Colour - Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI) as a reference, then aggregated into a Level-3 grid. Both, the mosaic and the reprojection were done using the Sentinel Application Platform (SNAP).
title: MODIS-Aqua Daily Rrs - OC-SMART AC
